last_transition_reason: The proof gives a complete incidence-variety/genericity argument matching the lemma sketch. It handles d=0 separately, shows each degree space V_i is nonzero, defines the strata X_J for possible support sets of nonzero common zeros, proves the dimension bound dim Y_J <= N-1 using the Hall-type hypothesis |I_J| >= |J|, deduces that tuples admitting a nonzero common zero on any stratum lie in a finite union of proper closed subsets of V, then uses Zariski density of k-rational points (k infinite) to choose a tuple over k outside that union. The weighted-homogeneous rescaling argument then shows any nonzero common zero would produce a point in some Y_J, contradiction. No substantive gap or semantic drift is present.
latest_nl_proof:
Let K be an algebraic closure of k. We must construct g_1, ..., g_d in k[x_1, ..., x_d] whose common zero locus in K^d is exactly {0}.

If d = 0, there are no polynomials to choose. The affine 0-space over K consists of one point, namely the origin, so the common zero locus of the empty family is exactly the origin. Thus the statement is trivial in this case.

Now assume d >= 1. Write [d] := {1, ..., d}. For each i, let V_i be the K-vector space of weighted-homogeneous polynomials of weighted degree e_i in K[x_1, ..., x_d], and let V := V_1 x ... x V_d. Taking J = [d] in the hypothesis, at least d of the d indices i satisfy e_i in Sigma([d]); hence in fact every e_i lies in Sigma([d]). Therefore each V_i is nonzero. Let N := dim_K(V).

For each nonempty subset J of [d], define I_J := { i in [d] : e_i belongs to Sigma(J) }. By hypothesis, |I_J| >= |J|. Choose once and for all an element a_J in J, and define
X_J := { x = (x_1, ..., x_d) in K^d : x_j = 0 for j not in J, x_j != 0 for j in J, and x_{a_J} = 1 }.
Then X_J is isomorphic to (K^*)^{|J|-1}, so dim(X_J) = |J| - 1.

Now consider the incidence set
Y_J := { ((f_1, ..., f_d), x) in V x X_J : f_i(x) = 0 for every i }.
We compute its dimension explicitly.

Fix J. For each i in I_J, choose a monomial M_{i,J} involving only variables x_j with j in J and having weighted degree e_i; this is possible because e_i belongs to Sigma(J). Choose a K-linear complement W_{i,J} such that V_i = K M_{i,J} direct_sum W_{i,J}.

If x belongs to X_J and i belongs to I_J, then M_{i,J}(x) != 0, because all variables indexed by J are nonzero on X_J. Hence every f_i in V_i can be written uniquely as f_i = c_i M_{i,J} + h_i with h_i in W_{i,J}, and the condition f_i(x) = 0 determines c_i uniquely from x and h_i, namely
c_i = - h_i(x) / M_{i,J}(x).
So for i in I_J, once x and h_i are chosen, there is exactly one choice of f_i with f_i(x)=0.

If i is not in I_J, then e_i is not in Sigma(J). Therefore no monomial of weighted degree e_i is supported only on the variables indexed by J. Hence every weighted-homogeneous polynomial of degree e_i vanishes on X_J (because on X_J all variables outside J are 0). So for i not in I_J there is no restriction at all on f_i.

Thus Y_J is isomorphic to
X_J x (product over i in I_J of W_{i,J}) x (product over i not in I_J of V_i).
Consequently,
dim(Y_J) = (|J|-1) + sum_{i in I_J}(dim V_i - 1) + sum_{i not in I_J} dim V_i
= N + |J| - 1 - |I_J|
<= N - 1,
because |I_J| >= |J|.

Let B_J be the Zariski closure in V of the projection of Y_J to V. Since dim(B_J) <= dim(Y_J) <= N-1 < N = dim(V), each B_J is a proper closed subset of the affine space V.

There are only finitely many nonempty subsets J of [d]. Since V is an affine space and therefore irreducible, the union of these finitely many proper closed subsets cannot be all of V. Hence
U := V \ (union over all nonempty J of B_J)
is a nonempty Zariski-open subset of V.

We now choose a point of U with coefficients in k. The space V is obtained from a finite-dimensional k-vector space by extending scalars to K, so after choosing a k-basis we may identify V with affine N-space over K, and its k-rational points are exactly the tuples of weighted-homogeneous polynomials with coefficients in k. Because k is infinite, k^N is Zariski dense in K^N (equivalently: a polynomial over K vanishing on all k-points must be the zero polynomial). Therefore U contains a k-rational point. Choose such a point and call it (g_1, ..., g_d). Then each g_i lies in k[x_1, ..., x_d] and has weighted degree e_i.

We claim that the common zero locus of g_1, ..., g_d in K^d is exactly {0}.

First, since each e_i is positive, each g_i has no constant term, so g_i(0)=0. Thus 0 is a common zero.

Conversely, let x = (x_1, ..., x_d) in K^d be a common zero of all g_i, and suppose x != 0. Let J := { j in [d] : x_j != 0 }. Then J is nonempty. Choose t in K such that t^{w_{a_J}} = x_{a_J}^{-1}; this exists because K is algebraically closed. Define y by y_j := t^{w_j} x_j for all j. Then y belongs to X_J: the coordinates outside J remain 0, the coordinates in J remain nonzero, and y_{a_J}=1.

Because each g_i is weighted-homogeneous of degree e_i,
g_i(y) = g_i(t^{w_1}x_1, ..., t^{w_d}x_d) = t^{e_i} g_i(x) = 0.
So ((g_1, ..., g_d), y) belongs to Y_J. Hence (g_1, ..., g_d) belongs to the projection of Y_J, and therefore belongs to its closure B_J. But we chose (g_1, ..., g_d) in U, so it lies in no B_J. This is a contradiction.

Therefore no nonzero common zero exists. Since 0 is a common zero, the common zero locus of g_1, ..., g_d in K^d is exactly the origin. This proves the lemma.
role_in_parent: Provides the actual degree-prescribed homogeneous equations once the Hall-type condition has been verified.
statement_nl: Let k be an infinite field, let d be a nonnegative integer, let w_1,...,w_d be positive integers, and let S = k[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_j)=w_j. Let e_1,...,e_d be positive integers. For each subset J of {1,...,d}, define Sigma(J) := { sum_{j in J} m_j w_j : each m_j is a nonnegative integer }. Assume that for every nonempty subset J of {1,...,d}, the set of indices i in {1,...,d} for which e_i belongs to Sigma(J) has cardinality at least |J|. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials g_1,...,g_d in S with deg(g_i)=e_i for each i such that, over an algebraic closure of k, the common zero locus of g_1,...,g_d in affine d-space is exactly the origin.

domain_restrictions: d is a nonnegative integer (note: behavior at d = 0 may need clarification)
for each j in 1..d, w_j is a positive integer
S is the polynomial ring k[x_1,..,x_d] with weighted grading where deg(x_j) equals w_j
for each i in 1..d, e_i is a positive integer
for any subset J of {1,..,d}, Sigma(J) consists of all integers that can be written as sum over j in J of m_j times w_j with each m_j a nonnegative integer
the hypothesis is required only for nonempty J
the conclusion about the common zero locus is evaluated after base change to an algebraic closure of k
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Assuming k is an infinite field, d is a nonnegative integer, w_1..w_d are positive weights defining a weighted grading on S = k[x_1,..,x_d], and e_1..e_d are positive integers such that for every nonempty subset J of {1,..,d}, at least |J| indices i satisfy that e_i can be expressed as a nonnegative-integer combination of the weights w_j with j in J, then there exist weighted-homogeneous polynomials g_1..g_d in S with weighted degrees deg(g_i) = e_i such that over an algebraic closure of k the set of common zeros of g_1,..,g_d in affine d-space consists exactly of the origin.
quantifier_order: for every nonempty subset J of {1,..,d}

there exist homogeneous polynomials g_1,..,g_d in S such that (1) deg(g_i) equals e_i for each i and (2) over an algebraic closure of k, the common zero locus of g_1,..,g_d in affine d-space is exactly the origin
